Judd Illusion

GeometryParadoxes
Game: A bar with arrow heads at both ends can look as though its two halves have different lengths.
How to play: Move the sliders to change the bar, its arrow heads and the mark in the middle. Tick the box to turn the mark into an arrow head, and drag the probe dot or use its arrow keys to read the halves.

Keyboard: Tab to the probe dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step). Every slider also takes arrow keys.

Look for the math

The cut-the-knot page says: "If the middle of a segment is marked by a short evenly (with regard to the two halves) spaced rectangle or a dot, the halves appear to have different lengths depending on the direction in which the arrow heads point. The illusion disappears or at least becomes less pronounced when the marker is replaced with an arrowhead." The live page embeds the applet at 500 x 400 with black ink on a white panel. What can be checked is the drawing: the two halves are equal in pixels whether or not the mark looks centred to your eye.

Where the middle mark sits

A line segment can be split into two equal halves, but the eye may disagree. On a canvas of width w, the applet sets c = round(w(100 − 2L)/200) and paints the bar from x = c − 20 to x = w − c − 20. The mark is drawn at x = trunc(w/2) − 20. On an even-width canvas that is exactly halfway: the two halves are both w/2 − c units long. At the opening settings (w = 500, L = 20) the bar runs from 130 to 330 and the mark sits at 230, so both halves are 100. The test checked all 36 lengths on 201 even canvas widths, 7,236 cases in all; every one had equal halves. Java's integer division truncates, so on an odd width the right half is one unit longer — the test confirms that exact one-unit difference for all 36 lengths at width 501. That is a rounding quirk of the original, kept here.

What the arrow heads do

Each arrow is drawn by the same Arrow routine, with h = +H or −H. If s is the sign of h, its strokes start at (x, mid − W·s) and end H units above or below at (x + A, mid − W·s − h); B parallel strokes, one unit apart, give it thickness. The two end arrows use the same x + A, so they always lean the same way: right when A > 0, left when A < 0, and straight up and down at A = 0. Changing H or A moves only the arrow strokes; the bar and its halves stay put. The test compared every one of the 101 heights times 181 slants with a second transcription of the bytecode, and checked the tip direction for all of them. This is the family of optical illusions that the page is showing.

Swapping the middle mark

With the box ticked, the applet's Bob routine paints B vertical strokes at x = trunc(w/2) − 20 + i, from mid − W − 3 to mid + W + 3. Unticking it paints two ordinary arrow strokes there instead. Nothing in the bar's rectangle or its two halves changes: the test compared a rectangle and an arrow-head mark across 2,268 size settings and found the bar identical every time. The page's other claim — that the illusion "disappears or at least becomes less pronounced" — is about what a person sees. No formula or pixel test can measure an impression, so this port does not pretend to have proved it; it gives you the switch to see for yourself.

The controls and a small quirk

The five sliders are the applet's five scrollbars, with exactly its ranges: L 10–45, W 0–20, H 10–110, A −90–90 and B 1–40. The opening picture uses the canvas fields L=20, W=5, H=50, A=10, B=10. One harmless quirk: the applet's A scrollbar is built at 30 but its value is never copied into the canvas until a control moves, so the first picture really uses A = 10. Our slider starts at 10 to agree with the picture. The site draws with its own ink and stage colours instead of the page's fcolor=000000, bcolor=ffffff, so both themes stay readable. The logic test also matched a second bytecode transcription over 756 length/thickness settings, 18,281 height/slant settings, 80 thickness/marker settings and 4,000 seeded joint configurations at six widths and four heights.

Try L = 45 and A = −90: the arrow heads turn left and their long strokes run off the edge, yet the probe still reads two equal halves.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
